issues.description: The authors explicitly state that cross-lagged path analysis is used to 'infer causal associations.' Cross-lagged panel models on observational data cannot establish causation; they can only establish temporal precedence of associations, which is consistent with but does not demonstrate causal effects. The design contains no manipulation, randomization, or control of confounders. This framing is repeated throughout and inflates the strength of conclusions.
issues.quote: We used cross-lagged path analysis to infer causal associations between SDO, RWA and willingness to sacrifice for the environment.

issues.description: The discussion asserts a causal pathway and even 'confidence in SDO having a causal effect.' These claims exceed what cross-lagged correlational data can support, especially given the authors themselves later acknowledge possible third-variable confounding. The contradiction between asserting causal effects and acknowledging confounds is internally inconsistent.
issues.quote: These results suggest that there is a causal pathway from ideological attitudes to environmentalism.

issues.subcategory: operationalization mismatch between construct and measure
issues.description: The title, abstract, and extensive discussion frame the work as about 'environmentalism' broadly and 'climate change' (denial, policy, environmental racism, IPCC effects), yet the dependent variable is operationalized with only two items measuring 'willingness to make sacrifices for the environment.' This narrow behavioral-intention measure does not capture the broad environmentalism construct discussed, leading to overgeneralized interpretations from a single narrow indicator.
issues.quote: Environmentalism was measured as individual’s willingness to make sacrifices for the environment.

issues.subcategory: mislabeling of standard error as standard deviation
issues.description: Path coefficients are reported with 'SD = .01' etc. For estimated regression/path parameters these values are standard errors (SE), not standard deviations. Mislabeling the precision statistic is an error that could mislead readers about the nature and computation of the uncertainty estimates.
issues.quote: the autoregressive path for willingness to sacrifice was strong (B = .83, SD = .01, p < .001, 95% CI [.82, .84])

issues.subcategory: internally inconsistent RMSEA point estimate and confidence interval
issues.description: The reported RMSEA point estimate of .03 falls outside its own reported 90% confidence interval of [.025, .026], whose upper bound (.026) is below the point estimate. A point estimate cannot lie outside its confidence interval; this is a reporting/computation inconsistency that undermines confidence in the fit reporting.

issues.subcategory: acceptance of model despite poor fit indices
issues.description: CFI = .86 is below conventional thresholds for acceptable fit (.90 minimum, .95 good), and SRMR = .07 is borderline. The authors selectively dismiss the poor-fitting indices as 'affected by model complexity' and accept the model based on indices they characterize as less complexity-sensitive. This is a selective interpretation of fit; CFI is not simply a complexity artifact and its poor value should be addressed rather than dismissed.
issues.quote: Overall, model fit was poorer for those indices affected by model complexity (e.g. χ2(2279) = 36511.73, p < .001, CFI = .86), however those less influenced by complexity pointed to good fit (RMSEA = .03, 90% CI [.025, .026], SRMR = .07), therefore the model was accepted.

issues.subcategory: unaddressed attrition and incorrect description of FIML
issues.description: A five-year longitudinal panel typically suffers substantial attrition, yet no retention rates, attrition analyses, or comparison of completers vs. dropouts are reported (deferred to a website). Additionally, FIML does not 'impute' missing data; it estimates parameters using all available information under a missing-at-random assumption. The MAR assumption and its plausibility given systematic attrition are not discussed.
issues.quote: Missing data were imputed using FIML.

issues.subcategory: measurement non-invariance from missing RWA item
issues.description: One RWA item was not administered at Time 2 but was at other waves, yet factor loadings and residual variances were constrained to equality across all time points. How the missing item at Time 2 was handled, and whether this disrupts the imposed longitudinal invariance constraints, is not explained. This affects the validity of the time-invariant model and comparability of the RWA latent variable across waves.
issues.quote: The item “Some of the best people in our country are those who are challenging our government, criticizing religion, and ignoring the “normal way” things are supposed to be done”, was not assessed at time two, but included in all other time points.

issues.description: The sample is described as 'nationally representative' and results as 'highly generalisable,' yet 62% female and 86% Pākehā suggest meaningful departures from the New Zealand population (which is roughly half female and has a larger non-European proportion). The strong generalizability claim is not reconciled with these compositional skews or with attrition-related selection.
issues.quote: Our research uses a nationally representative sample, meaning that our results are highly generalisable, at least to the New Zealand population.

issues.description: With N≈22,974, statistical significance is achieved for effects of negligible magnitude. The RWA→environmentalism cross-lagged path (B = -.02) and the environmentalism→RWA path (B = -.01) are extremely small. These are interpreted substantively (e.g., 'significant negative predictor', 'bidirectional association') without acknowledging that such effects may be practically meaningless. The emphasis on significance over effect size is a concern given the sample size.
issues.quote: SDO was a stronger predictor of change in environmental sacrifice (B = -.11, SD = .01, p < .001, 95% CI [-.13, -.09]) than RWA (B = -.02, SD = .01, p = .001, 95% CI [-.03, -.01]).

issues.description: The introduction states that Duckitt found 'relatively strong associations between SDO and RWA cross-sectionally in New Zealand,' attributed to political polarization, but the study's own Time 1 correlation is r = .21, which the authors elsewhere describe as the 'weak correlation typically found between SDO and RWA.' These characterizations are contradictory and the empirical data contradict the 'relatively strong' claim used to motivate the bidirectionality prediction.
issues.quote: Duckitt [3] shows relatively strong associations between SDO and RWA cross-sectionally in New Zealand, while in other contexts the relationship tends to be weaker or non-significant.

issues.description: The model imposes time-invariant factor loadings, intercepts, residual variances, latent means, and cross-lagged paths, justified by interest in overall effects rather than tested for appropriateness. Constraining latent means to equality assumes no mean-level change over five years, and constraining cross-lags assumes constant effects, both strong assumptions that, if violated, bias estimates. Whether these constraints fit the data (vs. a freely estimated model) is not reported, representing undisclosed analytic choices.
issues.quote: We imposed this stationary cross-lagged model because we were more interested in the overall and comparative effects of SDO and RWA on changes in environmentalism, and not on whether these effects change during the interval measured.

issues.subcategory: absence of pre-registration and post-hoc significance threshold
issues.description: No pre-registration is mentioned, and the significance threshold of p < .01 is adopted with reference to the large sample, but it is unclear whether this and other analytic decisions (constraint structure, choice of two-item DV, p threshold) were specified a priori. The combination of many flexible modeling decisions without pre-registration creates researcher-degrees-of-freedom concerns.
issues.quote: Because of the large sample size of this dataset, we adopted a conservative p-value threshold of p < .01 to indicate significance of findings (see also [30]).

issues.subcategory: overinterpretation of asymmetric cross-lag as socialization claim
issues.description: From the finding that RWA predicted SDO over time but not vice versa, the authors infer that 'New Zealanders are socialized into authoritarianism to a greater extent than social dominance.' This is a large theoretical leap from a small asymmetric path coefficient, with no measure of socialization processes, and is not supported by the data.
issues.quote: Because we found that RWA predicts SDO over time, but SDO does not predict RWA, this suggests that New Zealander’s are socialized into authoritarianism to a greater extent than social dominance.

issues.description: SDO (α = .69) and RWA (α = .70) reliabilities are low and based on only six abbreviated items each (three balanced pairs). Low reliability attenuates and can distort estimated associations, particularly when comparing the relative strength of SDO vs. RWA effects—a central claim of the paper. The differential reliability between scales is not addressed as a possible explanation for SDO appearing the 'stronger' predictor.
issues.quote: Reliabilities for SDO and RWA were poorer than is typically the case when the full scales are used, but are consistent with expectations based on previous research using short measures [31].

issues.subcategory: common method variance / single self-report method
issues.description: All three constructs are measured via the same self-report Likert format within the same survey at each wave. Shared method variance can inflate cross-construct associations and stability estimates, yet no procedural or statistical remedies (e.g., marker variables) are reported or discussed as a limitation affecting the cross-lagged estimates.
issues.quote: As our research was survey-based, participants’ responses were restricted to Likert-type responses to question items.

issues.subcategory: key sample and procedural details deferred to website
issues.description: Critical information needed to evaluate and replicate the study—retention/attrition rates across waves, sampling frame and response rates, and handling of the missing RWA item—is deferred to an external website rather than reported, hampering independent evaluation of the validity and generalizability of results.
issues.quote: Full details about the sample, including the procedure, retention, and demographics of participants, are available on the NZAVS website.

issues.description: A chi-square difference test for a single constrained parameter is reported as χ²(1) = 15,389.13, an extraordinarily large value for a 1-df comparison given the small parameter estimates involved (B = .02 vs B = -.001). Such a value warrants verification and explanation; as reported it strains credibility and is left uninterpreted beyond noting statistical difference.
issues.quote: These lagged effects were also statistically different (2(1) = 15,389.13, p < .001), a finding we explore more fully in the Discussion.

issues.subcategory: discussion content exceeding scope of data
issues.description: Extended discussion of environmental racism, IPCC projections, and disproportionate climate impacts on low-status groups is used to interpret a two-item willingness-to-sacrifice outcome, implying the data speak to these broad social-justice phenomena. This conceptual extrapolation links the narrow measured association to far-reaching real-world consequences not tested in the study.
issues.quote: Our findings therefore highlight Social Dominant’s way of thinking as having the potential to exacerbate environmental inequality, as the effects of unmitigated climate change disproportionately affect those lower in social status.
